source.title: The Quest of Finding the Antidote to Sparse Double Descent

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether regularization removes the double-descent pattern, but in a sparse-pruning setting rather than the size, epoch, or sample-size sweeps of the claim. Its results refine the regularization-dependence version.
record.gate_note: The paper measures test accuracy over iterative magnitude-pruning sparsity and reports how the sparse double-descent pattern changes with label-noise condition and ℓ2 regularization. These results are linked to V6 only. Its discussion of model-size and epoch-wise double descent and its cited results from other work are not results of this study. Table 1's selected-model performance and cost figures do not measure the curve, so they are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own iterative magnitude-pruning sweeps on ResNet-18 and ViT under label noise. It finds a non-monotonic test-accuracy curve over sparsity, which it describes as near an 'interpolation threshold'. It then varies ℓ2 strength λ on ViT and finds the peak removed. This is a new axis (sparsity from a trained dense model) with results bearing on V1 (model-size double descent, read via non-zero parameter count) and V6 (removal under tuned regularization). It is not a same-method replication.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors find sparse double descent in all tested setups. ℓ2 regularization can lessen or avoid it but sacrifices the performance/sparsity trade-off. Their knowledge-distillation scheme avoids it in the student model.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses iterative unstructured magnitude pruning with retraining and measures accuracy over sparsity, rather than sweeping model size, training epochs, or sample size as in the cited double-descent work.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pattern and its response to regularization vary with architecture, dataset, label-noise condition, and λ.

fits_no_version.finding: Knowledge distillation from a pruned or dense ResNet-18 teacher removes sparse double descent in a VGG-like student at all noise rates, while the vanilla student shows it (Fig. 5, Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distillation acting as a regularizer removes the double-descent peak along the sparsity axis.

record.peer_reviewed: PKDD/ECML Workshops; accepted for publication at the SCEFA workshop in conjunction with ECML PKDD 2023
record.problems: Curve values are presented in figures without numerical extraction in the text. The regularization ablation described here concerns ViT and sparse-pruning curves; the study does not establish a single mechanism linking label noise to the peak.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 reports VGG-like student sparse-pruning curves under vanilla training and distillation from pruned or dense teachers. Those results concern the paper's separate distillation scheme, not the ℓ2 regularization dependence recorded for V6, so they are not included as rows.

untested.parts: An explicit width/size sweep. Only the sparsity axis from pruning a trained dense model is used.
Varying the number of training samples.
Noise-free control (ε=0), so noise as the driver of the peak is untested. Variance mechanism, multiple descent, and regularization along the size, epoch and sample axes are also untested.

missing.what: Vanilla VGG-like student (γ=32, δ=5) shows sparse double descent at ε=10/20/50% on CIFAR-10/100. These are this study's own curves bearing on V1 along the sparsity axis.
Table 1 cost of λopt: 71.48% accuracy at 86.58% sparsity versus 74.47% at 99.26% for the full unregularized pruning process. Accuracy reaches random guess at >90% sparsity under λopt.

record.verdict_notes: Changes from the record: r1–r13 are also linked to V1, read along the sparsity axis. r14 is changed to cannot_determine. The record's V6 limits_scope label on r19–r20 is dropped: λ=1 is not the optimal λ at ε=50%, so their partial persistence fits V6. The V6 limits_scope now rests on the Table 1 trade-off cost, which is in the text but not in the rows. The claim that ResNet-18 keeps sparse double descent under ℓ2 is cited from the authors' prior work [37], not shown here, so it is not used. The study has no ε=0 condition, so noise as the driver of the peak cannot be assessed.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep and peak near the size that just fits the training set.
Changing training sample size near interpolation.
Capacity sweeps across model classes and the general double-descent curve.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations.

The study examines sparse double descent over pruning sparsity and regularization. It does not test whether noise causes the peak, variance as a mechanism, triple or multiple descent, or optimally tuned regularization across the original claim's model-size, epoch, and sample-size axes.
Recounting complexity using an effective number of parameters.

relationships.condition: Sparsity axis via iterative magnitude pruning, ResNet-18 and ViT, CIFAR-10/100/100N, noisy labels
relationships.reason: For all noise rates and both architectures, test accuracy over sparsity falls then rises again near the stated interpolation threshold (r1–r13). The analogue is along pruning sparsity, not trained-from-scratch size.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy decreased and then recovered around the stated interpolation threshold across all tested noise rates and both architectures as pruning sparsity increased.

source_check.reason: Section 3 reports the accuracy deterioration, recovery, and final deterioration over increasing sparsity for both architectures and all investigated noise rates; reversing the capacity axis gives the model-wise double-descent pattern.

relationships.condition: ViT, CIFAR-10/100, ε=10–50%, λ tuned per noise rate (λ=1 for ε≤20%, λ=3 for ε=50%)
relationships.reason: The peak seen at λ=0.03 (r8–r13) vanishes under tuned λ (r15–r18, r21–r22). Weaker λ=1 only mitigates it at ε=50% (r19–r20).
relationships.display_finding: Peaks at λ=0.03 disappeared with λ=1 for ε≤20% and λ=3 for ε=50%, while λ=1 only mitigated peaks at ε=50%.

source_check.reason: Section 4 and Figure 3 explicitly report disappearance at λ=1 for ε≤20% and monotonic performance at λ=3 for ε=50%; λ=1 only mitigates the latter.

relationships.condition: ViT, CIFAR-10, ε=10%, λopt versus unregularized full pruning (Table 1; from text, no row)
relationships.reason: Removing the peak with λopt costs accuracy and compressibility. Best accuracy is 71.48% at 86.58% sparsity versus 74.47% at 99.26%, and accuracy nears random guess above 90% sparsity.
relationships.display_finding: Peak removal yielded best accuracy of 71.48% at 86.58% sparsity, versus 74.47% at 99.26% sparsity with default λ=0.03 pruning, while accuracy approached random guessing above 90% sparsity.

source_check.condition: ViT, CIFAR-10, ε=10%, λopt versus unregularized full pruning (Table 1; from text, no row)
source_check.reason: Peak removal under λopt supports V6. V6 makes no promise about preserving accuracy or compressibility, so the reported cost does not limit its wording. The comparator is default λ=0.03 full pruning, not unregularized pruning.

relation.reason: Its own pruning sweeps demonstrate sparse double descent and test interventions that remove or mitigate it.

tranche.reason: The study tests double descent and regularization interventions in a pruning/retraining setting with sparsity as the capacity axis.

source_check.notes: The λopt values are the authors' selected settings; the text does not establish a common pointwise risk-optimal tuning protocol. Sparse double descent is measured over pruning sparsity, with retraining after each pruning step.

statements.correction: ViT/CIFAR-10, ε=10%: full pruning with the default λ=0.03 yields 74.47±0.01% accuracy at 99.26% sparsity; λopt yields 71.48±0.06% at 86.58% sparsity. Peak removal has a performance/compressibility cost.
statements.problem: The performance and sparsity cost is reported, but the full-pruning comparator uses λ=0.03, not zero regularization. V6 does not promise cost-free peak removal.
